messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Layla's Burden

Layla was forty-six when she came to the clinic, her dark eyes rimmed with exhaustion, her posture held so rigidly upright it seemed to cost her something. She worked as a pharmacist at a busy retail chain in suburban Michigan, a job she had held for nearly two decades with quiet competence, but in the past three years something had fractured in her. The breaking point, she said, came when her son Amir was nine years old.

It had started with a fever that wouldn't break—ordinary enough, she thought, the way a mother thinks when she is still able to believe in the ordinariness of things. But the fever spiked higher, and then came the rash, and within hours the pediatrician's face had shifted into the expression Layla would later recognize as the moment everything changed. Meningitis. The ambulance ride—she remembered the siren cutting through her like a blade, remembered sitting beside Amir's small body as it convulsed, remembered the certainty that bloomed in her chest that this was the moment she would lose him. He spent five days in the pediatric intensive care unit. He survived. But Layla did not return from that hospital intact.

The first year after Amir's recovery, she had tried to move forward. He was fine now, the doctors said. Fully recovered. But Layla had come to believe something different about herself in those hospital corridors. She was weak—had she not been helpless, paralyzed, able to do nothing while her child suffered? And if she was weak, if she had failed to protect him even when she was present, what good could possibly lie ahead for either of them? She was defective in some fundamental way, a mother who could not keep her own child safe. The thought circled endlessly, and with it came the conviction that nothing good would happen to her anymore, that she was marked somehow by what she had witnessed.

These beliefs had begun to reshape how she moved through the world. Any reminder of that hospital—the sight of an ambulance passing on the street, the smell of antiseptic in her own pharmacy, the sight of a child in a hospital gown on television—sent her into a state of such intense vigilance that her body could not settle. Her heart would race. Her shoulders would climb toward her ears. Because she believed she was weak, because she was certain that catastrophe was always waiting, Layla had started to avoid the very spaces and cues that might trigger these sensations. She stopped visiting her sister when the sister was hospitalized for routine surgery. She began calling in other pharmacists to cover shifts when her workplace received deliveries of pediatric medications. She would not go to her nephew's soccer game because the field was near a medical clinic, and the mere possibility of seeing an ambulance in the distance made her throat close.

The more she avoided, the more her sense of threat intensified. Her body had learned that the world was dangerous, and avoidance had become the only way she knew to buy herself a few hours of relative calm. But that calm was fragile and shrinking. At night, she lay awake for hours, her mind refusing to settle, her body taut as a wire. When she finally drifted toward sleep, the smallest sound—a car door slamming, a siren blocks away—would jolt her awake, her heart hammering as though she were back in that hospital room. She jumped at the ring of the pharmacy phone. She flinched at her own name called across a room. The constant state of readiness, the belief that danger was imminent and that she was too weak to face it, had become exhausting beyond measure.

What troubled her most was how her avoidance had begun to confirm her darkest beliefs about herself. Her sister had stopped asking her to visit. Her ex-husband, with whom she shared custody of Amir, had gently suggested that perhaps she should see someone because Amir was starting to ask why his mother seemed so afraid all the time. Each time she avoided a situation, each time her body flooded with panic and she retreated, she felt the proof settling deeper: she was broken, she could not handle ordinary life, nothing good would come of this. The cycle had tightened until she could barely recognize the capable, steady woman she had been before the hospital. It was this—the slow dissolution of her sense of self, the way her attempts to protect herself from harm had instead imprisoned her—that finally brought her to seek help.
